The Golden-lined spinefoot (Siganus lineatus) is a tropical rabbitfish widely distributed across the Indo-Pacific, where it inhabits coral reefs and adjacent seagrass beds. Adult body size in this species is highly variable, with the maximum recorded ultimate total length reaching 43 cm [Li = 43 cm], representing the upper bound of somatic growth. A detailed morphometric survey conducted across multiple reef sites in the Philippines indicated that the standard length at which 50 percent of individuals become reproductively active is 28 cm [Lp = 28 cm], a value that aligns closely with estimates from congeneric species. Using a length-weight conversion factor of 0.01698, the calculated wet weight corresponding to this pubertal length is approximately 373 grams [Wwp = approximately 373 grams], while the asymptotic body mass is 1350 grams [Wwi = 1350 grams]. These mass estimates place Siganus lineatus among the medium-bodied members of the genus and are consistent with the energetic demands of an herbivorous fish that forages on benthic algae throughout daylight hours.

Under controlled laboratory conditions where water temperature was maintained at a stable 28 °C [T = 28 °C], investigations into early life history revealed that embryonic development proceeds rapidly. Hatching of the fertilised egg occurs after approximately 2.5 days [ab = approximately 2.5 days], a brief incubation period that is typical for tropical teleosts with smal at a temperature of 28 °C [T = 28 °C]l pelagic eggs. The wet weight at birth, derived from a mean egg diameter of 0.55 millimeters, is calculated to be about 0.000087 grams [Wwb = about 0.000087 grams], reflecting the minute size of the newly emerged yolk-sac larva. During this lecithotrophic phase, the prolarva relies entirely on endogenous yolk reserves and remains largely inactive, drifting within the water column until the onset of first exogenous feeding approximately three to four days post-hatching.

Reproductive output in Siganus lineatus has been characterised through field observations of spawning aggregations in the Ryukyu Archipelago at a water temperature of 28 °C [T = 28 °C]. The frequency of these spawning events has been estimated at approximately 365 events per year [F_R_i = approximately 365 events per year], reflecting the capacity for nearly daily spawning during peak activity periods. This elevated spawning frequency, which is higher than that reported for most other siganid species, suggests an adaptation to the predictable availability of planktonic food resources for the resulting pelagic larvae.

This lifespan is comparable to that reported for Siganus fuscescens, a closely related congener with broadly overlapping ecological requirements. The age-based demographic data suggest that annual natural mortality rates are relatively low for a fish of this body size, likely due to the species' possession of venomous dorsal spines that deter many potential predators. Seasonal patterns in somatic condition, measured via hepatosomatic and gonadosomatic indices, indicate that energy reserves are maximal just prior to the monsoon-driven spawning peaks.

The juvenile phase following larval metamorphosis and benthic settlement is characterised by extremely rapid somatic growth, with young-of-year fish attaining a total length of approximately 12 to 15 cm within their first twelve months. Field studies employing otolith microchemistry and daily increment analysis have confirmed that the transition from the pelagic larval stage to the benthic juvenile stage occurs between 21 and 28 days post-hatching, after which the growing fingerling adopts the herbivorous diet of the adult. These sub-adult fish typically inhabit shallow reef flats and seagrass meadows, where they form loose aggregations that provide protection from piscivorous predators. The high annual reproductive rate observed in Siganus lineatus, combined with its relatively short generation time, makes the species resilient to moderate levels of fishing pressure, although population declines have been documented in regions where heavy exploitation of spawning aggregations occurs.
